title: Salute to Women Inventors
summary: Josh and Chuck salute women inventors whose work was overlooked, starting with the barrier that women could not hold patents easily (coverture, no property rights) and Charlotte Smith's push for a list of women patent holders in the 1880s. They profile Marie Van Brittan Brown's home security system, Josephine Cochrane's dishwasher, Marion Donovan's diaper cover and disposable diaper, Margaret Knight's flat-bottom paper grocery sack and safety shuttle stop, Mary Anderson's windshield wiper, and Margaret Wilcox's railway car heater. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about episode titles.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with playful banter and introduce the episode on overlooked women inventors and the barriers they faced.

segments.title: Barriers for women inventors and Charlotte Smith's patent list
segments.summary: Women held about ten percent of patents in the late twentieth century. Many filed under male relatives because of coverture and lacked property rights and technical education. Economic feminists tied self-sufficiency to suffrage. Charlotte Smith pushed the Patent Office to compile a list of women patent holders, published in 1888 in 500 copies.

segments.title: Early women patent holders
segments.summary: Mary Dixon Kies is cited as the first American woman to earn a patent in her own name, about ninety years before the list.

segments.title: Marie Van Brittan Brown's home security system
segments.summary: Nurse Marie Van Brittan Brown, with her electronics technician husband Albert Brown, patented a closed circuit TV home security system in 1966 with a sliding camera, four peepholes, two-way microphones, remote door lock and emergency button. She died in 1999 and 32 later patents cited it.

segments.title: Josephine Cochrane and the dishwasher
segments.summary: Wealthy socialite Josephine Cochrane invented a practical dishwasher after her servants chipped her fine china, patented December 28, 1886, and won a World's Fair award in 1893. Her company later became KitchenAid. Hotels adopted it first, and home use grew by the 1950s.

segments.title: Dishwasher tangent
segments.summary: Casual talk about vacation houses with two dishwashers and drawer-style dishwashers, tied back to Cochrane.

segments.title: Marion Donovan and disposable diapers
segments.summary: Marion Donovan, a homemaker and former Vogue worker, made a waterproof diaper cover from a shower curtain, then parachute nylon, called the Boater. It sold at Saks Fifth Avenue in 1949, Keko Corporation offered a million dollars, and she patented it in 1951. Her disposable diaper did not sell until Procter and Gamble launched Pampers about ten years later. She also invented the Zippity Do and the Big Hang Up closet grid and designed her house after a Yale architecture degree at 41.

segments.title: Margaret Knight and the flat-bottom paper grocery sack
segments.summary: Margaret Knight worked in a textile mill as a child and invented a device that stops machinery and a shuttle guard. At Columbia Paper Bag Company she designed a square-bottom paper grocery sack and a machine to make it in 1870. When Charles Annan copied her idea, she won a patent interference suit and received her patent in 1871, going on to hold more than twenty patents.

segments.title: Mary Anderson and the windshield wiper
segments.summary: Alabama inventor Mary Anderson, after seeing New York streetcar drivers struggle with snow, invented a lever-operated windshield wiper. Cadillac made it standard starting in 1922. Later she built an apartment building in Birmingham and ran a ranch and vineyard in Fresno.

segments.title: Margaret Wilcox and the car heater
segments.summary: Margaret Wilcox invented a system to pipe engine heat to railway passenger cars, patented in 1893. Engineers later adopted the principle for enclosed automobiles. Hosts compare it to Volkswagen Beetle heaters and discuss the earlier women's patent list, and Wilcox's unpatented clothes dishwasher-combination idea.

segments.title: Listener mail on episode titles
segments.summary: A listener from Norway, Morton Laggerud, and a listener in DC share funny misunderstandings of episode titles such as Hobo Signs and Conductors. Hosts invite listeners to send emails to the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and plug the iHeartRadio app.
